keenable.snippet:
# Living in a “High-Crime Area” Is Not Probable Cause: The Fourth Circuit’s Decision in United States v. Griffin
By / September 18, 2026
On August 14, 2026, the Fourth Circuit threw out a 180-month sentence because the search warrant that produced the evidence never should have issued. *United States v. Griffin* is a significant win for anyone who cares about what police must actually prove before a judge lets them through the front door of a home. The court’s message is direct: a neighborhood’s reputation is not a substitute for facts about a particular house.
## The Warrant and the Search
Calvert County’s Drug Enforcement Unit sought a no-knock warrant for a residence in a small Maryland community the affidavit called an “open-air drug market.” The supporting affidavit ran twenty-one pages. It described decades of drug sales in the area, listed criminal histories, and recounted surveillance from the preceding months.
Officers executed the warrant and found no drugs inside the home. What they did find was in a locked SUV parked beside the house: cocaine, marijuana, and a firearm. A jury later acquitted Earl Griffin, Jr. of the drug and firearm-trafficking counts but convicted him of being a felon in possession. The district court denied his motion to suppress, conceding the affidavit “may not be the strongest” it had read while finding it good enough.
## Nexus: Proximity Is Not Enough
The Fourth Circuit disagreed, and its reasoning rests on two requirements every residential warrant must satisfy: nexus and timing.
Nexus means the affidavit must connect the evidence sought to the specific place searched. Drug activity near a home is relevant, but the court reaffirmed that proximity alone will not do. The affidavit needed additional facts—that a dealer lived there and kept drugs there, left the house to make a sale, returned after one, retrieved drugs from inside, or carried proceeds in. None of that appeared.

linkup.title: Living in a "High-Crime Area" Is Not Probable Cause: The Fourth Circuit's Decision in United States v. Griffin - The Chetson Firm
linkup.snippet:
On August 14, 2026, the Fourth Circuit threw out a 180-month sentence because the search warrant that produced the evidence never should have issued. *United States v. Griffin* is a significant win for anyone who cares about what police must actually prove before a judge lets them through the front door of a home.
Calvert County’s Drug Enforcement Unit sought a no-knock warrant for a residence in a small Maryland community the affidavit called an “open-air drug market.” The supporting affidavit ran twenty-one pages. It described decades of drug sales in the area, listed criminal histories, and recounted surveillance from the preceding months.  
Officers executed the warrant and found no drugs inside the home. What they did find was in a locked SUV parked beside the house: cocaine, marijuana, and a firearm. A jury later acquitted Earl Griffin, Jr. of the drug and firearm-trafficking counts but convicted him of being a felon in possession. The district court denied his motion to suppress, conceding the affidavit “may not be the strongest” it had read while finding it good enough.
For anyone whose home was searched on a warrant, *Griffin* is a reminder that the affidavit is the case. Ask what it actually alleges about your residence, as opposed to your street, your relatives, or your neighbors. Ask how old those allegations are.

United States v. Earl Griffin, Jr. (4th Cir. Aug. 14, 2026) (published) — Reversed, vacated, and remanded (Benjamin, J.; Gregory, J., joined; Heytens, J., dissenting).
1. Introduction
  
    United States v. Earl Griffin, Jr. is a Fourth Amendment decision about the minimum constitutional showing needed to search a home for drug evidence.

octen.title: Search and seizure - Search warrant application provided insufficient basis to search premises - Virginia Lawyers Weekly
octen.snippet:
Background
A federal grand jury convicted Earl Leroy Griffin, Jr. of being a felon in possession of a firearm. The defendant’s challenge to the search warrant requires this court conduct two inquiries: (A) whether the application gave the issuing judge a substantial basis to find probable cause to search the 6740 residence and, if it did not (B) whether the officers relied in “good faith” on the issuing judge’s probable cause determination such that the evidence should nevertheless be admitted.
Probable cause
There must be some nexus between the suspected crime and the place to be searched.” In addition to a physical nexus, probable cause also requires a fair probability that evidence of the suspected crime will be found in the place to be searched at the time of the search. The affidavit here failed to establish a fair probability that contraband or evidence of a crime would have been found in the 6740 residence at the time of the search because the facts set forth in the affidavit were either (1) not connected to the 6740 residence, (2) too old or (3) both.
First, the affidavit’s broader allegations may have described drug activity in the area, but they did not supply a connection between that drug activity and the 6740 residence. The more recent August observations also failed to connect recurrent Kent Bottom drug activity to the 6740 residence.
The lack of concrete connection to the 6740 residence is important because the Fourth Amendment does not permit suspicion by geography.

seltz.snippet:
On August 14, 2026, the Fourth Circuit threw out a 180-month sentence because the search warrant that produced the evidence never should have issued. *United States v. Griffin* is a significant win for anyone who cares about what police must actually prove before a judge lets them through the front door of a home. The court’s message is direct: a neighborhood’s reputation is not a substitute for facts about a particular house.

## The Warrant and the Search

Calvert County’s Drug Enforcement Unit sought a no-knock warrant for a residence in a small Maryland community the affidavit called an “open-air drug market.” The supporting affidavit ran twenty-one pages. It described decades of drug sales in the area, listed criminal histories, and recounted surveillance from the preceding months.

Officers executed the warrant and found no drugs inside the home. What they did find was in a locked SUV parked beside the house: cocaine, marijuana, and a firearm. A jury later acquitted Earl Griffin, Jr. of the drug and firearm-trafficking counts but convicted him of being a felon in possession. The district court denied his motion to suppress, conceding the affidavit “may not be the strongest” it had read while finding it good enough.

## Nexus: Proximity Is Not Enough

The Fourth Circuit disagreed, and its reasoning rests on two requirements every residential warrant must satisfy: nexus and timing.

Nexus means the affidavit must connect the evidence sought to the specific place searched. Drug activity near a home is relevant, but the court reaffirmed that proximity alone will not do. The affidavit needed additional facts—that a dealer lived there and kept drugs there, left the house to make a sale, returned after one, retrieved drugs from inside, or carried proceeds in. However, the court held that the district court erred on refusing to put the question of proper venue to the jury. The court noted that multiple circuits found that venue is a jury question when (1) the defendant objects to venue prior to the close of the prosecution’s case, (2) there is a genuine issue of material fact on proper venue, and (3) the defendant timely requests a jury instruction. # Living in a “High-Crime Area” Is Not Probable Cause: The Fourth Circuit’s Decision in United States v. Griffin
By / September 18, 2026
On August 14, 2026, the Fourth Circuit threw out a 180-month sentence because the search warrant that produced the evidence never should have issued. *United States v. Griffin* is a significant win for anyone who cares about what police must actually prove before a judge lets them through the front door of a home. The court’s message is direct: a neighborhood’s reputation is not a substitute for facts about a particular house.
## The Warrant and the Search
Calvert County’s Drug Enforcement Unit sought a no-knock warrant for a residence in a small Maryland community the affidavit called an “open-air drug market.” The supporting affidavit ran twenty-one pages. It described decades of drug sales in the area, listed criminal histories, and recounted surveillance from the preceding months.
Officers executed the warrant and found no drugs inside the home. What they did find was in a locked SUV parked beside the house: cocaine, marijuana, and a firearm. A jury later acquitted Earl Griffin, Jr. of the drug and firearm-trafficking counts but convicted him of being a felon in possession. The district court denied his motion to suppress, conceding the affidavit “may not be the strongest” it had read while finding it good enough.
## Nexus: Proximity Is Not Enough
The Fourth Circuit disagreed, and its reasoning rests on two requirements every residential warrant must satisfy: nexus and timing.
Nexus means the affidavit must connect the evidence sought to the specific place searched. Drug activity near a home is relevant, but the court reaffirmed that proximity alone will not do. The affidavit needed additional facts—that a dealer lived there and kept drugs there, left the house to make a sale, returned after one, retrieved drugs from inside, or carried proceeds in. None of that appeared.
